etm. The word originates from Greek [[8]] words "" as in "Tool," and "" as in "Shock" or "Realization"

In Greek, what are words for "Tool" and "Shock, Revelation or Recognition?" 

definition: The existential shock; A realization that a tool has real-world power; both for good and for harm. An emphemeral state in which a tool momentarily crosses the threshhold between "inatimate object" and "difference between life and death."

pragma: In the context of a survival situation; a flashlight could be the difference between a person "seeing in the dark" or not. That kind of technology is deeply undervalued; so much so, that when it enters the forefront of consciousness; it is somewhat traumatizing and relieving. Almost like a "trust" or "dependency" on this otherwise "lifeless material." This creates an existential weight where there existed no such previously; tools are not inatimate; they are effectively extensions of our Autonomy; such that the Pragmatics, Circumstance and Ethics often define the tool more than it's very own nature; i.e., fire can either harm, or it can burn rope. Suggesting tools are not "function enclosed by lifeless form"... rather, tools are defined by those wielding them; the severity of the situation; the dependency on the tool, and the pragmatics; Ethics of consequential effects.

Ultimately, resulting in a shift of perspective; a tool is no longer "just a replaceable material thing"... in modern life, much of the everyday human life is dependent almost entirely on some form of tool; whether firsthand interaction, or dependency on a clockwork or system of tools. All built by someone else; a network of communication. 

All of that is encoded in a humble little hammer-and-nail; or a match-and-box. Tools carry within them, sparks of the extensions of Autonomy that once birthed them by necessity; Tools encode historical reason. If we want to learn about a Civilization; we study their tools; Languages, Societies, Systems, Architecture, Cultures, Rituals, etc. that's a form of Existential recognition worth naming.

Of course; the word should not overstep territory either; tools are extensions of Autonomy; but fundamentally incomplete without Ethics, Pragmatics and Consequential results of Tool-making decisions.

This is especially true in the age of "Invisible toolchains" where tools have become increasingly interdependent on one-another; and communication is becoming more and more distanced.

That's a discussion for another day.
